planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil along a woodland edge, hedgerow, or shrub border; Huron tolerates just a few hours of direct sun per day and still flowers and fruits well.

directions: Huron is a compact, rounded selection of gray dogwood bred for a tidier habit than the often-suckering wild species. White flower clusters open in spring and are followed by white berries on red stalks that birds strip quickly, while the deep green summer foliage turns burgundy-red in fall. It adapts to a wide range of soils, shrugs off urban air pollution, and is best rejuvenated by cutting a few of the oldest stems to the ground each year rather than shearing the whole plant. Thin out root suckers periodically if a tighter, non-spreading form is desired.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade beneath an open tree canopy.

directions: Squirt is a dwarf selection of coastal doghobble that stays under two feet tall while still spreading into a broad, low mound, making it useful where the full-size species would outgrow a woodland border. Glossy evergreen leaves emerge mahogany and copper before settling into deep hunter-green, and small white bell-shaped flowers line the arching stems in spring. It needs no regular pruning and works well as an understory companion to azaleas and rhododendrons on shaded slopes. Honeybees visit the spring flowers, and the dense evergreen cover offers year-round shelter for small wildlife.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial sun to partial shade; it spreads slowly by rhizomes into an evergreen mat and needs little intervention once established.

directions: Berried Treasure is a fruiting-focused selection of the rare, boxwood-leaved box huckleberry, a dwarf evergreen groundcover that spreads into broad colonies over time rather than staying as a single clump. Small bell-shaped spring flowers give way to dark, blueberry-like fruit that birds and foragers both seek out, and the glossy foliage takes on red tones in winter. It performs well as a slow-spreading groundcover on shaded slopes or in rock gardens, and once settled in requires only minimal pruning to keep it tidy. Its low, spreading habit makes it a good substitute for non-native evergreen groundcovers in woodland-edge plantings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average to dry, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; group several together for a low hedge or mass planting.

directions: Forever Emerald is a dwarf inkberry holly selection that forms a tight, naturally rounded mound without the legginess or bare lower branches common to older inkberry cultivars. Its small, boxwood-like dark green leaves hold their color through winter, and inconspicuous spring flowers give way to small black berries that persist into the colder months. It tolerates hard pruning if needed but generally keeps its neat shape without shearing, making it a low-maintenance substitute for non-native boxwood in foundation plantings or edging. Deer tend to leave it alone, and the winter berries offer a modest food source for birds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall on a shaded, well-drained slope in organically rich, consistently moist, acidic soil; a thick mulch layer helps keep roots cool through summer.

directions: Independence is a selection of native rosebay rhododendron, the large understory shrub that forms dense evergreen thickets in Appalachian cove forests, chosen for reliable clear pink flowers that open in early July, later than most rhododendrons. Long, leathery, strap-shaped leaves stay evergreen year-round and give the plant a substantial woodland presence even in winter. It is best sited on a shaded slope where water drains away from the roots, since rosebay rhododendron resents standing water despite wanting consistent moisture. Once established, it needs only light pruning after bloom and offers dense cover and nesting habitat for songbirds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates heavy clay and seasonally saturated sites better than most flowering trees.

directions: Moon Glow is a sweetbay magnolia selection valued for its evergreen-to-semi-evergreen habit in milder zones, holding onto more of its shiny, dark green, silver-backed leaves through winter than the species typically does further north. Creamy white, lemon-scented flowers open in late spring with sporadic rebloom into summer, followed in fall by knobby red seed cones that draw songbirds. It is one of the few flowering trees genuinely happy with wet feet, making it a strong choice for rain gardens, pond edges, or low spots that stay consistently moist. In colder parts of its range, siting it out of harsh winter wind helps it hold its foliage longer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average to consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Misty Blue is a foliage-forward selection of white baneberry (doll's eyes), grown as much for its soft, finely cut, blue-green leaves as for its display of white berries with a single black dot that follows the May flower spikes. The berries sit on bright red stalks and persist for a month or more into fall, giving strong seasonal interest in a shaded woodland garden. It is a slow-spreading, multi-stemmed clump former, best left undisturbed once sited correctly rather than divided often. As with the species, every part of the plant is toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas where children or pets might sample the showy berries.
